sections.h2: Who bills and who hears appeals for property tax in Bergen County, NJ?
sections.html:
Bergen County does not send your bill. Each of its 70 municipalities, the most of any New Jersey county, values its own parcels through a local assessor and collects through a local tax collector. The county's role is the Bergen County Board of Taxation at Two Bergen County Plaza, 1st Floor, in Hackensack, which hears assessment appeals. Its number is 201-336-6300.

Hackensack is the county seat. The county covers 246 square miles in the northeast corner of the state, from the Hudson Palisades in the east to the Ramapo Mountains in the northwest. The Hackensack and Saddle rivers, the Meadowlands in the south and three drinking water reservoirs shape much of the land. Because the municipality sets value and sends the bill, the town where the house sits decides who you deal with.

sections.h2: How big is the Bergen County housing market for sellers?
sections.html:
It is the largest county in New Jersey by population, with 955,732 residents in the 2020 census and an estimate of 977,026 for 2025. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures show how pricey and settled the market is.

  • Median value of owner occupied homes: $623,000.
  • Median household income: $124,884.
  • Owner occupied rate: 65.3 percent, with 372,622 housing units as of July 2025.
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $3,547, and $1,498 without one.
  • Median gross rent: $1,914.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 2,970.

The economy leans on health care and corporate offices. Hackensack University Medical Center is listed as the largest employer, and the county's gross domestic product was $81.5 billion in 2022, the highest in the state. About 91 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

sections.h2: What makes Bergen County locations different for house sellers?
sections.html:
Bergen County sits in the New York City metropolitan area. The George Washington Bridge links Fort Lee to Upper Manhattan and is described as the world's busiest motor vehicle bridge. The county also holds the northern end of the New Jersey Turnpike and the Garden State Parkway, the eastern end of Interstate 80, part of Interstate 287 and routes 3, 4, 17 and 208. Workers spend a mean of 31.2 minutes getting to their jobs, according to the Census Bureau.

Roads total nearly 2,989 miles, and the municipalities maintain about 2,403 of them. Streets, school districts and assessments differ from one borough to the next, so ask the municipal assessor and the county board for your town's average assessment ratio, and ask how the town's last revaluation affected similar homes.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Bergen County assessment?
sections.html:
You file a petition with the Bergen County Board of Taxation, and the county asks people to use its online filing option. Appeals are due each year on or before April 1, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of assessment notices, or by May 1 where the town carried out a revaluation or reassessment. The county's own page notes that the 2026 deadline has passed, so the next window opens with the 2027 notices.

Checkpoints for a Bergen County assessment appeal
CheckpointRule
Assessment dateOctober 1 of the year before the tax year
Filing deadlineApril 1, or May 1 after a revaluation
Evidence at filingComparable sales of 3 to 5 similar properties
Copies to assessor and boardAt least 7 days before the hearing
Board decisionWithin 3 months of the filing deadline
FreezeValue set on appeal holds for the assessment year and the next 2

Source: New Jersey Division of Taxation, A Guide to Tax Appeal Hearings.

The county tells filers the current assessment is presumed correct, so you carry the burden of proving it is too high. A bill cannot be appealed, because the tax comes from the local budget. Only the assessment can be challenged.

sections.h2: What evidence works at a Bergen County tax hearing?
sections.html:
Evidence of market value as of October 1 of the pretax year. The state's guide stresses that sales used for comparison should come before that date, and the assessments of similar houses cannot be used as proof.

  • Three to five sales of properties like yours, attached to the petition.
  • Photographs of your house and the comparable houses.
  • An income statement, if the property is commercial.
  • Repair estimates or an appraisal if the house has defects.

Plan to attend. Adjournments are usually denied, and a no show can lead to a judgment for lack of prosecution that blocks a later appeal to the Tax Court of New Jersey. Where a town has not done a recent revaluation, the board also tests your assessment against a common level range of plus or minus 15 percent of the district's average ratio. The county's Board of Taxation lists that ratio for each town.

sections.h2: Can older Bergen County homeowners get a tax deduction?
sections.html:
Yes, a $250 deduction is available to residents who are 65 or older, or disabled, and have lived in New Jersey at least a year. You must own and occupy the home on October 1 of the pretax year and stay under the state's income limit. Surviving spouses and civil union partners aged 55 or older can qualify too.

File Form PTD with the local assessor or tax collector, then send Form PD5 to the tax collector each year by March 1 to keep the deduction. If the town denies it, appeal to the county board on Form A-1 by April 1 of the year after the denial. The Division of Taxation's Property Administration unit answers questions at 609-292-7974 or 609-292-7975.

sections.h2: What does a Bergen County owner pay at closing for taxes?
sections.html:
The title company or closing attorney asks your town's tax collector for the status of every quarter. New Jersey towns bill in installments, and in Brick, for example, those dates are February 1, May 1, August 1 and November 1. Bergen towns each publish their own collector page, so ask yours which quarters are paid and how any unpaid balance and interest stand.

  • The seller usually covers taxes up to the closing date, and the buyer covers the rest. The contract sets the split.
  • Added or omitted assessments for new work can trigger an extra bill, so mention any addition you built.
  • An appeal still pending at closing should be addressed in the contract, since a refund belongs to whoever paid the tax.

For numbers, call the municipal collector or the Bergen County Board of Taxation. The county posts each year's tax rates and equalization tables on its website.

faqs.q: Who do I pay property tax to in Bergen County?
faqs.a: Pay your municipal tax collector, not the county. Bergen County has 70 municipalities, and each one has its own collector, bill and payment methods. The county board in Hackensack only handles assessment appeals.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal in Bergen County?
faqs.a: The filing deadline is April 1 each year, or within 45 days of the bulk mailing of notices. It moves to May 1 where the town did a revaluation or reassessment. The county's website says the 2026 deadline has passed.

faqs.q: Where is the Bergen County Board of Taxation?
faqs.a: It is at Two Bergen County Plaza, 1st Floor, Hackensack, NJ 07601, and the phone number is 201-336-6300. The office accepts filings in person, though the county urges owners to file online.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss my Bergen County tax appeal hearing?
faqs.a: The board can enter a judgment for lack of prosecution, and that can block a later appeal to the Tax Court of New Jersey. The state's guide says adjournments are ordinarily denied, so plan to attend.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Bergen County house with an unpaid tax quarter?
faqs.a: Yes. Unpaid taxes and interest are paid from your proceeds at closing, and the title company gets the payoff from the municipal collector. Ask the collector for the amount before you set a closing date.
